nameStory: The mapleleaf viburnum gets its name from its distinctive three-lobed leaves that look remarkably like those of a maple tree. It's also called maple-leaved arrowwood, since Native Americans and early settlers used its straight, flexible stems to make arrow shafts. The alternate name 'dockmackie' comes from old regional dialect, though its exact origins are lost to time.
description: Mapleleaf viburnum is a low-growing deciduous shrub that typically reaches 3-6 feet tall, making it one of the smaller viburnums in New England. It has the distinctive maple-like leaves that give it its name, along with flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in spring. In fall, it produces dark blue-black berries and often displays beautiful pink to deep red foliage colors. This woodland shrub tends to form colonies through underground runners, creating patches in the forest understory.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves that strongly resemble maple leaves, with a soft, velvety texture underneath that feels almost fuzzy to the touch. The leaves are opposite on the stem and turn brilliant pink, red, or purple in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters about 2-4 inches across, appearing in late spring. Each tiny flower has a sweet, mild fragrance when you get close.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dark blue to black berries in late summer that are flattened rather than round, sitting in loose clusters. The berries have a somewhat dry, mealy texture and are not particularly tasty to humans.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading shrub that rarely exceeds 6 feet tall, often forming colonies through underground runners. The stems are relatively straight and flexible, with a smooth grayish bark.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed winter buds that are reddish-brown and sit opposite each other on the stems. The buds have a few visible scales and help identify the plant when leafless.

habitat: Mapleleaf viburnum thrives in the dappled shade of deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, preferring well-drained but moist soils. You'll often find it on slopes, in woodland clearings, and along forest edges, typically growing alongside other understory shrubs like witch hazel and elderberry. It's particularly common in oak-hickory forests and can tolerate fairly dry conditions once established.

seasonality.spring: New leaves unfurl with a soft, light green color, and flat-topped clusters of small white flowers appear in late May to early June. The flowers have a subtle sweet fragrance that attracts various small pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with distinctive three-lobed maple-like foliage that remains green through the season. Small green berries begin developing after the flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Spectacular fall color ranging from pink to deep red or purple, often more vibrant than many maples. Dark blue-black berries ripen and provide food for birds before leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show the opposite branching pattern and small reddish-brown buds. Old berry clusters may persist, and the low, spreading growth habit becomes clearly visible.

funFact: Despite being called 'mapleleaf' viburnum, this shrub is actually more closely related to elderberries than to maple trees, and its maple-like leaves are a perfect example of convergent evolution - where unrelated plants develop similar features independently!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young maple trees due to the three-lobed leaves, but remember that viburnum leaves are opposite while maple leaves are also opposite - the key difference is that this stays a low shrub and has the white flower clusters typical of viburnums. If you see maple-like leaves on a plant that never gets taller than your waist, it's likely mapleleaf viburnum.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'arrowwood' appears in several viburnum species because many viburnums have straight, flexible stems that were prized for making arrows and other tools. However, each species earned this name independently, so 'arrowwood' doesn't indicate a close relationship between different viburnum species.
compareHints: Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves. It's also notably smaller than most other viburnums like nannyberry or hobblebush, staying under 6 feet tall. The soft, velvety underside of the leaves is another unique feature among our local viburnums.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
